planting.note: Start transplants or plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; willowleaf aster naturally grows at the wetter, sunnier edge of prairies and marshes and tolerates periodic flooding better than most asters.

directions: Start transplants or plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; willowleaf aster naturally grows at the wetter, sunnier edge of prairies and marshes and tolerates periodic flooding better than most asters. Narrow, willow-like leaves clothe tall, upright stems that spread gradually by rhizome into loose colonies, topped in fall by masses of small, lavender-blue, yellow-centered daisy flowers that are an important late-season nectar source for migrating monarch butterflies and native bees. Native to wet prairies, marsh edges, and low meadows across the central and eastern United States, it is a strong choice for the moist portion of a pollinator garden or the sunnier fringe of a rain garden where it can spread without crowding out smaller neighbors. Cut stems back in late winter before new growth resumes, and divide congested clumps every three to four years.

planting.note: Start transplants or plant divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas ironweed is more compact and better behaved in a garden border than the larger, coarser ironweed species.

directions: Start transplants or plant divisions in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Texas ironweed is more compact and better behaved in a garden border than the larger, coarser ironweed species. Slender, upright stems carry narrow leaves and flat-topped clusters of small, intensely purple, fringed flowers from late summer into fall, drawing swallowtails, skippers, and other butterflies in large numbers during a season when many other nectar plants have finished blooming. Native to open prairies, woodland edges, and roadsides across Texas, Oklahoma, and Louisiana, its smaller stature compared to relatives like New York and giant ironweed makes it a better fit for mixed perennial borders and smaller pollinator gardens. It is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond cutting stems back in late winter.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost, or set out transplants, in lean, well-drained, sandy to caliche soil in full sun; Drummond's sundrops thrives on poor, dry soils and rots quickly in rich, wet, or heavily amended ground.

directions: Direct sow after last frost, or set out transplants, in lean, well-drained, sandy to caliche soil in full sun; Drummond's sundrops thrives on poor, dry soils and rots quickly in rich, wet, or heavily amended ground. Low, sprawling, gray-green stems bear narrow leaves and a long succession of bright lemon-yellow, four-petaled flowers that open in late afternoon and evening and fade to orange-red by the next morning, a color-changing habit that adds interest across a single planting. Native to sandy prairies, coastal plains, and dry roadsides across Texas and the south-central United States, it flowers from spring through fall in a single season, often behaving as a short-lived perennial or reseeding annual in the garden. Extremely heat- and drought-tolerant once established, it needs no supplemental water or fertilizer and is an excellent low, spreading filler for a xeriscape or rock garden.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; Texas pink skullcap is a Mexican drylands native that rots in heavy, poorly drained, or overwatered soil.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, gravelly to sandy, very well-drained soil in full sun; Texas pink skullcap is a Mexican drylands native that rots in heavy, poorly drained, or overwatered soil. Fine, needle-like evergreen foliage forms a dense, tidy mound smothered from spring through fall in small, tubular, cherry-pink to magenta flowers that are a magnet for bees and hummingbirds throughout the long Gulf South growing season. Native to limestone slopes in northeastern Mexico, it is exceptionally heat- and drought-tolerant once established, thriving in the reflected heat of a rock garden, dry border, or xeriscape bed where it needs no deadheading to stay in near-continuous bloom. Shear lightly in late winter to remove any cold-damaged growth and keep the mound compact.

planting.note: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; Wright's skullcap is a Texas Hill Country limestone native that needs sharp drainage and struggles in humid, poorly drained conditions.

directions: Plant container-grown transplants in spring in lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; Wright's skullcap is a Texas Hill Country limestone native that needs sharp drainage and struggles in humid, poorly drained conditions. Small, gray-green leaves form a low, dense mound studded with two-lipped, violet-blue flowers held on short spikes from spring through summer, providing season-long nectar for native bees on some of the thinnest, rockiest soils in a xeriscape planting. Endemic to limestone outcrops and rocky slopes of central Texas, it is exceptionally drought-tolerant once established and thrives in crevice or rock gardens where richer soil would cause it to rot. Shear lightly after the first flush of bloom to encourage repeat flowering and keep the mound tidy.

planting.note: Plant divided bulb clusters in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wakegi onion is a sterile hybrid grown only from bulb divisions, never from seed, and multiplies quickly into a clump that can be split every year.

directions: Plant divided bulb clusters in fall in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; wakegi onion is a sterile hybrid grown only from bulb divisions, never from seed, and multiplies quickly into a clump that can be split every year. A traditional Japanese hybrid between bulb onion and bunching onion, it produces slender, mild-flavored, scallion-like stalks from a clustering base of small bulbs, combining the easy perennial habit of a bunching onion with a slightly stronger, more onion-like flavor. Harvest by pulling whole young stalks as needed through fall, winter, and spring in mild climates, leaving several bulbs in place to keep the clump multiplying, or dig and divide the whole clump every one to two years to maintain vigor and share starts. It is far less prone to bolting than seed-grown bunching onions and provides a reliable, low-effort source of fresh green onions for most of the year.
sources: Slow Food International Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into loose, deep, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; sand palafox is adapted to shifting coastal and inland dunes and performs poorly in heavy clay or richly amended soil.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into loose, deep, well-drained sandy soil in full sun; sand palafox is adapted to shifting coastal and inland dunes and performs poorly in heavy clay or richly amended soil. Tall, slender stems carry narrow, fuzzy gray-green leaves and are topped from late summer into fall with airy clusters of pink to lavender, fringed, thistle-like composite flowers that are a strong late-season draw for bees and butterflies. Native to deep sand dunes, sandhills, and disturbed sandy ground across the western Gulf coastal plain and adjacent Texas sand sheet, it is an excellent choice for stabilizing loose, dry, sandy sites where few other showy wildflowers will grow. It self-sows readily in sandy soil once established and needs no irrigation or fertilizer beyond its first few weeks of establishment.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; pricklyleaf dogweed thrives on poor, dry, caliche soils and needs no fertilizer or supplemental watering once established.

directions: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, rocky to gravelly, alkaline, very well-drained soil in full sun; pricklyleaf dogweed thrives on poor, dry, caliche soils and needs no fertilizer or supplemental watering once established. Finely divided, aromatic, thread-like foliage forms a low, dense mound studded with small, bright yellow, daisy-like flowers over an unusually long season from spring through fall, drawing small native bees and butterflies to even the driest, rockiest corner of a garden. Native to limestone outcrops, caliche flats, and dry plains across Texas and the southwestern United States, it is a tough, long-lived, low-maintenance filler for rock gardens, gravel gardens, and xeriscape borders. Established plants need no irrigation beyond natural rainfall and resent rich, moist, or heavily mulched soil.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; slender scratchdaisy is native to open sandy coastal plain habitats and performs poorly in rich, heavily amended, or poorly drained garden soil.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into lean, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; slender scratchdaisy is native to open sandy coastal plain habitats and performs poorly in rich, heavily amended, or poorly drained garden soil. Wiry, branching stems carry narrow leaves and a long late-summer-through-fall succession of small, bright yellow, daisy-like flowers that provide a reliable nectar source for native bees and small butterflies as many other Gulf coast wildflowers finish for the season. Native to sandy pinelands, coastal prairies, and disturbed open ground across the western Gulf coastal plain, it self-sows readily in loose sandy soil, behaving as a short-lived perennial or reseeding annual in the garden. It needs no supplemental irrigation or fertilizer once established and is a useful, easy-care filler for a sandy meadow or pollinator planting.
